MINUTES
  ADJOURNED CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  POLICY DEVELOPMENT SESSION
  MARCH 30, 2026

1.  CALL MEETING TO ORDER

An adjourned meeting of the City Council of the City of Rolling Hills Estates was called to order
at 12:09 p.m. in the Council Chamber, 4045 Palos Verdes Drive North, by MAYOR ZERUNYAN.

2.  SALUTE TO THE FLAG

Led by Administrative Aide Gabrielle Swain.

3.  ROLL CALL

City Council Members Present:  Brown Schachter, Huff, Schmitz, Stegura, Zerunyan

City Council Members Absent:  None

City Staff Present:  City Manager Greg Grammer
  City Attorney Don Davis
  Assistant City Manager Alexa Davis
  Administrative Services Director Mike Whitehead
  Community Dev/Public Works Director Jeannie Naughton
  City Clerk Lauren Pettit
  Assistant to the City Manager Jessica Slawson
  Public Works Manager Kirsten Graham
  Senior Accountant Fernando Estrada
  Community Services Supervisor Rosa Pinuelas
  Administrative Aide Gabrielle Swain

4.  PUBLIC COMMENT / PUBLIC PRESENTATION

A.  KNN PUBLIC FINANCE - S&P GLOBAL RATING STATUS AND DEBT MANAGEMENT
  POLICY

Senior Accountant Estrada introduced consultant Mark Young from KNN Public Finance, who
provided an update on the City’s S&P Global Ratings credit rating, including an overview of the
City’s current credit profile, factors that influence the rating, and how the rating impacts the City’s
financial position and future borrowing opportunities:

Consultant Mark Young from KNN Public Finance introduced the proposed Debt Management
Policy, establishing clear guidelines for the issuance and management of debt, ensuring that any
future borrowing or debt financung is conducted in a prudent and transparent manner.

Discussion ensued regarding the City’s recent AA+ credit rating from S&P, highlighting it as a
strong result that reflects solid finances, strong demographics, and effective fiscal management..
The rating positions the City well for future borrowing, particularly for projects like the Nature
Center and street improvements. To support this, the city is developing a formal debt
management policy—based on best practices from other high-rated cities—to guide how debt is
issued, managed, and kept compliant with legal requirements. Council Members asked clarifying
questions about the policy’s scope, investment rules, and applicability to related entities, and
raised concerns about flexibility in emergency situations, such as infrastructure failures. Staff
and the consultant indicated the policy allows some flexibility and can be amended, with reserves
intended as the first response to emergencies. The policy will be further refined with the Budget
Subcommittee and brought back for final approval in June.

B.  SOUTH BAY REGIONAL HOUSING TRUST

South Bay Cities Council of Governments (SBCCOG) Executive Director Jacki Bacharach and
Senior Program Manager Ronson Chu presented an overview of the South Bay Regional Housing
Trust (SBRHT) for City Council’s consideration, outlining the requirements and benefits of
becoming a participating member of the regional trust.
ADJOURNED CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  1
MARCH 30, 2026 (PDS)
 Discussion ensued regarding the proposed South Bay Regional Housing Trust. The consultant
confirmed that joining the trust would have no dues initially, and participation would give the City a
seat at the table to shape policies and access tools not available through the COG, such as
financing affordable housing projects, preserving existing affordable units, providing rent subsidies,
and offering technical services like income verification. While Director Bacharach emphasized
benefits like regional collaboration, assistance for seniors and essential workers, and potential
funding opportunities, Council Members questioned the direct value to a largely built-out city with
limited development capacity and mostly moderate-income projects (which the trust currently
cannot fund without legislative changes). There was general consensus to move forward with
participation, with staff to return with a formal agreement and designation of a delegate and
alternate representative to the Trust’s Board for approval at the next City Council meeting.

5.  MID-YEAR ACCOMPLISHMENTS

A.  DEPARTMENTAL MID-YEAR STAFF REPORTS

  Recommendation: That the City Council receive and file these reports.

Administrative Services Department mid-year accomplishments provided by Senior Accountant
Estrada (as per the agenda material).

Administration Department mid-year accomplishments provided by Assistant City Manager
Davis (as per the agenda material), which included a Public Outreach Overview presentation.

Community Services Department mid-year report provided by Assistant City Manager Davis and
Community Services Supervisor Pinuelas (as per the agenda material).

Community Development mid-year accomplishments provided by Community Development &
Public Works Director Naughton (as per the agenda material).

Public Works Department mid-year accomplishments provided by Community Development &
Public Works Director Naughton (as per the agenda material).

  MAYOR PRO TEM SCHACHTER moved, seconded by COUNCIL MEMBER SCHMITZ,
  TO APPROVE AS:

  RECEIVE AND FILE THE MID-YEAR REPORTS.

MAYOR ZERUNYAN so ordered.

6.  POLICY DEVELOPMENT SESSION ITEMS

A.  ADMINISTRATIVE SERVICES DEPARTMENT:
  FINANCE UPDATE, INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY UPDATE, CYBERSECURITY

  Recommendation: That the City Council consider the items presented and prioritize them
  on the work plan for the coming fiscal year.

  FINANCE UPDATE

Senior Accountant Estrada provided a staff report (as per the agenda material), providing an
update on the City’s main audit activities, highlighting that the City’s auditors are progressing
well on the annual audit and financial report, with preliminary work scheduled for late April and
final completion expected around October. The City also received a Government Finance
Officers Association (GFOA) Certificate of Achievement for its 2024 financial report, with 2025
results pending, and no issues were found in a recent revenue review. During discussion,
MAYOR PRO TEM SCHACHTER requested historical data on revenue received from the Peter
Weber Equestrian Center (which pays the City 10% of income), and staff agreed to provide a
multi-year breakdown to support future contract considerations at the upcoming Budget
Workshop.

This item is informational for the Council.

ADJOURNED CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  2
MARCH 30, 2026 (PDS)
   INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY UPDATE

Administrative Services Director Whitehead provided a staff report (as per the agenda material),
providing a high-level update on the City’s cybersecurity measures including ongoing efforts to
strengthen cybersecurity through improved systems, staff training, third-party assessments, and
coordination with state and federal partners. Staff emphasized continued vigilance and
education to protect City data and systems.

This item is informational for the Council.

  FISCAL HEALTH REPORT

Senior Accountant Estrada presented the City’s Fiscal Health Report, providing a
comprehensive ten-year perspective on key financial trends relevant to the City of Rolling Hills
Estates. The Fiscal Health Report indicated the City remains in a strong financial position, with
property tax revenues increasing by 3.1% and sales tax expected to remain stable. Expenditures
have grown modestly, with public safety as the top priority.

  COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA moved, seconded by MAYOR PRO TEM SCHACHTER,
  TO APPROVE AS:

  RECEIVE AND FILE THE FISCAL HEALTH REPORT.

MAYOR ZERUNYAN so ordered.

B.  ADMINISTRATION DEPARTMENT:
  ELECTRONIC BICYCLES (E-BIKES) OUTREACH AND REGULATIONS, MAYORAL
  ROTATION, CITY COUNCIL CONFERENCE ATTENDANCE, SB 707 COMPLIANCE,
  WASTE MANAGEMENT CONTRACT, ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) USE UPDATE

  Recommendation: That the City Council consider the items presented and prioritize them
  on the work plan for the coming fiscal year.

  ELECTRONIC BICYCLES (E-BIKES) OUTREACH AND REGULATIONS

Assistant to the City Manager Slawson provided a staff report (as per the agenda material).

Discussion ensued regarding ongoing e-bike safety concerns and the need for a local ordinance
consistent with neighboring cities like Rancho Palos Verdes to improve safety and provide
enforcement tools. While there was agreement on the importance of safety, Council Members
expressed concerns about enforceability, limited Sheriff resources, and unintended
consequences, such as discouraging safe transportation to school or penalizing parents riding
with children.

Following discussion, it was the consensus of the City Council to direct staff to move
forward with a draft ordinance, to include the following:
  • Require e-bike riders to yield to pedestrians
  • Require passengers to have proper seating (no unsafe multi-rider situations)
  • Require riders to travel single file or no more than two abreast
  • Prohibit racing, stunt riding, and unsafe maneuvers (e.g., wheelies)
  • Consider enhanced penalties for violations
  • Ensure consistency with California Vehicle Code and nearby cities’ regulations

  MAYORAL ROTATION

City Manager Grammer provided a staff report (as per the agenda material).

Discussion ensued revisiting the City Council’s Mayoral rotation practice, which traditionally
places newly elected members in the fifth seat, typically requiring five years before becoming
Mayor. Some Council Members advocated changing this to allow a shorter path (e.g., four years)
and placing new members in the fourth seat, maintaining it better reflects prior service,
encourages participation, and aligns with democratic expectations. Others raised concerns
about protecting the City from potential instability, particularly in scenarios where multiple new

ADJOURNED CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  3
MARCH 30, 2026 (PDS)
 members could quickly assume leadership and emphasized the importance of experience and
safeguards.

Following discussion, it was the consensus of the City Council to direct staff to develop
a formal Mayoral Rotation Policy, incorporating placement of outgoing Mayors in the fifth
seat, new members in the fourth seat along with provisions to maintain Council discretion
and include a minimum amount of service on the City Council before becoming Mayor.

  CITY COUNCIL CONFERENCE ATTENDANCE

City Clerk Pettit provided a staff report (as per the agenda material).

Discussion ensued, affirming the value of attending conferences for training, networking, and
regional collaboration, while noting that participation is already budgeted (around $21k–$25k
annually). Some Council Members raised concerns about rising registration costs, others
emphasized the importance of continued participation, noting it enhances the City’s influence
and leadership opportunities. There was also support for annual planning and coordination, such
as providing an annual overview of conferences and allowing Council Members to indicate
attendance in advance. Overall, the Council supported continuing current practices, improving
coordination, and communicating concerns about costs, without restricting participation.

This item is informational for the Council.

  WASTE MANAGEMENT CONTRACT

Assistant City Manager Davis provided a staff report (as per the agenda material), noting that
Waste Management has expressed interest in extending the agreement ahead of its 2029
expiration, prompting the City to begin analysis and negotiations. Staff is working with a
consultant and will bring findings to the Waste Subcommittee and later the full Council, along
with a proposed annual rate increase of about 4.9% (plus a small commercial adjustment).

Discussion ensued regarding the possibility of regional coordination with other Peninsula cities,
though challenges were noted due to the City’s unique services (e.g., free recycling/green waste,
manure collection, and clean-air trucks), which may limit compatibility and cost benefits. While
some concern was raised about rising costs and past pricing issues, others emphasized that
prior analyses showed the current contract remains competitive and that alternative providers
are limited.

Following discussion, it was the consensus of the City Council to direct staff to continue
evaluation and negotiations, with staff to report back after further analysis.

  ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) USE UPDATE

Assistant City Manager Davis provided a staff report (as per the agenda material), noting that
staff is increasingly using generative AI tools to assist with tasks such as drafting emails, staff
reports, social media content, and meeting materials, while maintaining human oversight for final
content. The City is currently testing and comparing multiple platforms (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot,
Claude, Fireflies, Canva) and exploring additional applications like note-taking, minutes
preparation, and public records research tools. Staff is also engaging with external partners and
coalitions to stay informed on best practices, governance, and vetted vendors, while holding
internal discussions to evaluate practical use cases. Overall, the update emphasized that AI is
being adopted as a support tool to improve efficiency, with ongoing evaluation and no immediate
policy changes needed.

This item is informational for the Council.

  SB 707 COMPLIANCE

City Attorney Davis provided a staff report (as per the agenda material), summarizing the new
state legislation requirements related to public meetings, particularly a July 1 deadline mandating
enhanced remote participation capabilities. The City is upgrading its AV system to include
interactive video and telephone access, minor website updates, providing guidance on language
access (though no translation services are required), and developing outreach efforts to
encourage broader public participation.
ADJOURNED CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  4
MARCH 30, 2026 (PDS)
 This item is informational for the Council.

C.  COMMUNITY SERVICES DEPARTMENT:
  LANDSCAPE CONTRACT, TREE MAINTENANCE CONTRACT, MUNICIPAL CODE
  UPDATES, COMMUNITY SERVICES FEE STUDY, CITY 70TH ANNIVERSARY,
  PROJECT UPDATES AND PARK IMPROVEMENTS

  LANDSCAPE CONTRACT

Assistant City Manager Davis provided a staff report (as per the agenda material), noting that
the City has reached the end of its allowed extensions with its current provider, Bennett
Landscape, which has served the City since 2009. As a result, staff plans to issue a new Request
for Proposals (RFP) in the coming months to establish a contract starting July 1. While the
process will be competitive, Bennett will be invited to submit a proposal and could continue as
the provider if selected.

Following discussion, it was the consensus of the City Council to direct staff to issue a
new RFP for the City’s Landscape contract.

  TREE MAINTENANCE CONTRACT

Assistant City Manager Davis provided a staff report (as per the agenda material).
recommending a one-year extension with West Coast Arborists, citing their strong performance
and good coordination with City staff. The extension includes a modest price increase already
anticipated in the budget.

Council Members also raised concerns about tree trimming done by Southern California
Edison’s contractor (Davey’s), noting inconsistent and often excessive pruning. Staff explained
that while the City does not control Edison’s work, they have been improving coordination to
minimize impacts and can respond to resident concerns by inspecting or addressing affected
trees.

Following discussion, it was the consensus of the City Council to direct staff to move
forward with a one-year extension to the contract with West Coast Arborists for continued
services for FY 2025-26 and an increase of 5% (for a total increase of 8%) to the budget
in the next two fiscal years to enhance tree maintenance services.

  MUNICIPAL CODE UPDATES

Community Services Supervisor Pinuelas provided a staff report (as per the agenda material)
regarding horse-related trail use. Staff proposes clarifying the municipal code regarding wheeled
and motorized vehicle use on equestrian trails, noting a mismatch between the current code,
which broadly prohibits all wheeled vehicles, and long-standing practice, which allows limited
motorized access for equestrian-related purposes (e.g., hay deliveries, manure removal,
veterinary services).

Concerns were raised about misuse, such as residents driving personal vehicles on trails under
loosely interpreted justifications. The Council agreed that the code should be updated and more
clearly defined to prohibit non-essential or recreational vehicle use while explicitly allowing
legitimate equestrian-support activities

Following discussion, it was the consensus of the City Council to direct staff to return
with revised ordinance language for consideration.

Community Services Supervisor Pinuelas provided a staff report (as per the agenda material)
regarding park-use regulations, aiming to codify existing practices and address gaps in the
municipal code. Key updates include prohibiting unauthorized private instruction in parks (while
allowing permitted or city-contracted programs), allowing amplified sound and commercial
activity only with approved permits, and clarifying rules such as banning e-bikes. A major focus
was on open flame use, where the code currently lacks guidance.

Council Members expressed support for allowing limited, safer options like small propane grills
in designated areas, while prohibiting higher-risk activities such as charcoal or open flame fires
ADJOURNED CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  5
MARCH 30, 2026 (PDS)
 due to wildfire concerns and disposal issues. Regarding ceremonial burns (e.g., flag retirement),
the Council preferred not banning them entirely but directing them to safer alternatives, such as
coordination with the Fire Department or designated facilities (i.e. Fire Station 106).

Following discussion, it was the consensus of the City Council to direct staff to draft
ordinance updates that: prohibit unauthorized private lessons while allowing permitted
programs; allow amplified sound and sales only with event approval; ban e-bikes;
establish clear open-flame rules, allowing only propane grills in designated areas while
prohibiting charcoal and open fires; allow for ceremonial flag retirement burns only under
safer, controlled conditions (e.g., coordination with the fire department) and consider
restrictions like no burning on red flag days, ensuring the code is clear and enforceable.

  COMMUNITY SERVICES FEE STUDY

Community Services Supervisor Pinuelas provided a staff report (as per the agenda material),
noting that while fees have been adjusted incrementally over time, a full review has not been
done recently. Matrix Consulting has been engaged to evaluate cost recovery, market rates, and
comparisons with other cities, and preliminary findings have been received. Staff will finalize the
report and bring it back to the Council later in the spring after review by relevant committees,
with no action required at this time.

This item is informational for the Council.

  CITY 70TH ANNIVERSARY

Community Services Supervisor Pinuelas provided a staff report (as per the agenda material),
recommending a modest approach consistent with past practice for non-major milestones. Staff
suggested instead of hosting new events, the City will recognize the anniversary through
branding efforts, such as a commemorative logo and promotional items throughout the year.

Council Members agreed this aligns with how previous anniversaries (e.g., 60th and 65th) were
handled, reserving larger celebrations for major milestones like the upcoming 75th anniversary.

This item is informational for the Council.

  PROJECT UPDATES AND PARK IMPROVEMENTS

Community Services Supervisor Pinuelas provided a staff report (as per the agenda material),
noting that while a list of improvements has been identified and is being reviewed with advisory
committees, most projects will be deferred to future fiscal years due to larger ongoing capital
priorities unless urgent needs arise.

During discussion, Council Members highlighted specific items, including progress on the
Chandler Park fence project and the need to prioritize replacement of the equestrian harrow,
which is heavily used and may not be durable long-term. There was also discussion of a potential
ADA assessment at Chandler Park, particularly regarding ramp access, restrooms, and future
amenities, though this has been deferred as funding is currently focused on the Nature Center.

This item is informational for the Council.

D.  COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT:
  ZONING CODE UPDATES, DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS, LONG-RANGE PROJECTS
  AND PROGRAMS

  ZONING CODE UPDATES

Community Development Director Naughton provided a staff report (as per the agenda material),
highlighting amendments across 16 chapters to improve clarity and consistency. Key updates
include creating standardized procedures for permits, public hearings, appeals, ongoing
housing-related code updates (especially ADUs) to stay compliant with state law, and advancing
implementation of a workforce housing overlay zone adopted in the General Plan.

This item is informational for the Council.
ADJOURNED CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  6
MARCH 30, 2026 (PDS)
   DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS

Community Development Director Naughton provided a staff report (as per the agenda material),
noting that the 927 Deep Valley Drive (La Sevilla) project has received its certificate of
occupancy and is about 30% sold, with staff assisting in marketing the moderate-income units.
The Brick Walk Residences project is still in process, awaiting a parcel map application and
undergoing limited environmental review focused on biological resources due to streamlined
state requirements.

This item is informational for the Council.

  LONG -RANGE PROJECTS AND PROGRAMS

Community Development Director Naughton provided a staff report (as per the agenda material),
including an update on long-range planning and infrastructure initiatives, including ongoing work
to update the landmark overlay district ordinance, with a draft expected before the end of the
fiscal year, and a broader historic preservation program to follow. Staff is also preparing to
update the General Plan Safety Element in response to the Hazard Mitigation Plan, potentially
coordinating with neighboring cities to share resources. Additionally, the City is participating in
a Clean Power Alliance “Power Ready” program to evaluate solar, battery storage, and backup
power at City Hall as a critical facility.

This item is informational for the Council.

E.  PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT:
  STORMWATER PROJECT UPDATES, PROJECT UPDATES

  STORMWATER PROJECTS UPDATE

Community Development & Public Works Director Naughton provided a staff report (as per the
agenda material), including drywell projects, the Torrance Airport Stormwater Basin project, the
Palos Verdes Peninsula Multi-Benefit Flow Diversion feasibility study, and the stormdrain repair
program.

This item is informational for the Council.

  PUBLIC WORKS PROJECTS UPDATE

Public Works Manager Graham provided a staff report (as per the agenda material), highlighting
progress and funding efforts. The George F Canyon Nature Center project is underway but still
has a funding gap. The Rolling Hills Road Multi-Modal Project is fully designed and funded, with
outreach planned in 2026 and construction expected in 2027. The Rollingwood sidewalk repair
project will proceed soon, while the FY 2026–27 street resurfacing program is being deferred to
coordinate with other major projects. The Dapplegray/PVDN intersection improvement project is
fully funded, out to bid, and scheduled for construction over summers 2026–2027. The City also
secured $1.5M in safety grants for guardrails and pedestrian improvements, with timing aligned
to minimize disruptions. The Peter Weber Equestrian Center restroom project continues to
progress through complex permitting, with staff working toward final approvals.

This item is informational for the Council.
